questions.question: What is const_cast in C++ and when should it be used?
options: Converts between unrelated pointer types with no safety checks

Removes or adds const/volatile qualifiers from a pointer or reference — should only be used when the underlying object was originally non-const and you need to call a non-const API; using it to modify a truly const object is undefined behavior
Converts floating point values to integer with truncation
Performs safe downcast in an inheritance hierarchy at runtime
questions.answer: Removes or adds const/volatile qualifiers from a pointer or reference — should only be used when the underlying object was originally non-const and you need to call a non-const API; using it to modify a truly const object is undefined behavior

questions.question: What is std::move() in C++ and what does it actually do to the source object?
options: std::move() physically moves data from one memory location to another

std::move() is a cast to rvalue reference — it does NOT move anything itself; it enables move semantics by allowing the move constructor/assignment to steal resources from the source, leaving the source in a valid but unspecified state
std::move() calls the destructor of the source object immediately
std::move() swaps two objects using three copy operations
questions.answer: std::move() is a cast to rvalue reference — it does NOT move anything itself; it enables move semantics by allowing the move constructor/assignment to steal resources from the source, leaving the source in a valid but unspecified state

questions.question: What is RTTI in C++ and which two operators use it?

RTTI is only available when the class implements a virtual getType() method manually
RTTI is disabled by default and must be enabled with a special compiler pragma
questions.answer: RTTI (Run-Time Type Information) allows querying an object's actual dynamic type at runtime — used by dynamic_cast (safe polymorphic downcast) and typeid (retrieve std::type_info); requires at least one virtual function in the class

questions.question: What is the difference between function overloading and default arguments in C++? When do they cause ambiguity?

Overloading defines multiple functions with different parameter lists; default arguments give parameters fallback values — ambiguity occurs when a call matches both an overloaded function and a defaulted version, causing a compilation error
Default arguments replace overloading entirely in modern C++
Ambiguity only occurs with virtual functions, not regular overloads
questions.answer: Overloading defines multiple functions with different parameter lists; default arguments give parameters fallback values — ambiguity occurs when a call matches both an overloaded function and a defaulted version, causing a compilation error

A destructor is only needed for classes that use inheritance

questions.question: What is a class template in C++ and how does it differ from a function template?

Class templates only work with STL containers
Function templates require explicit type specification; class templates deduce automatically
questions.answer: A class template defines a blueprint for a generic class parameterized by one or more types; a function template defines a generic function — class templates need explicit instantiation type (e.g., Stack<int>), function templates can deduce the type from arguments

list provides O(1) random access; vector does not
vector uses more memory than list for all sizes
questions.answer: vector stores elements in contiguous memory enabling O(1) random access but O(n) insertion/deletion in the middle; list is a doubly-linked list with O(1) insert/delete anywhere but no random access (O(n) traversal)

A namespace only affects the visibility of class member functions

questions.question: What are inline functions and what is the trade-off when overusing them?

Inline functions are a compiler hint to replace the call site with the function body — benefit: eliminates function call overhead; trade-off: excessive inlining increases binary code size (code bloat), potentially degrading cache performance
Inline functions cannot have loops or conditional statements
Inline functions always improve performance with no downsides
questions.answer: Inline functions are a compiler hint to replace the call site with the function body — benefit: eliminates function call overhead; trade-off: excessive inlining increases binary code size (code bloat), potentially degrading cache performance

questions.question: What is the difference between single and multiple inheritance in C++?
options: Single inheritance is safer; multiple inheritance is not allowed in C++

Single inheritance: a class inherits from exactly one base class; multiple inheritance: a class inherits from two or more base classes — multiple inheritance can cause the diamond problem if not handled with virtual inheritance
Multiple inheritance can only be used with abstract base classes
Single and multiple inheritance behave identically in C++
questions.answer: Single inheritance: a class inherits from exactly one base class; multiple inheritance: a class inherits from two or more base classes — multiple inheritance can cause the diamond problem if not handled with virtual inheritance

questions.question: What is the purpose of the 'override' keyword in C++11?

override explicitly signals that a function is intended to override a base class virtual function — the compiler emits an error if no matching virtual function exists in the base, preventing silent signature mismatches

override prevents the function from being further overridden in subsequent subclasses
questions.answer: override explicitly signals that a function is intended to override a base class virtual function — the compiler emits an error if no matching virtual function exists in the base, preventing silent signature mismatches

questions.question: What is the difference between compile-time polymorphism and runtime polymorphism in C++?
options: They are identical — all polymorphism is resolved at compile time

Compile-time polymorphism (function/operator overloading, templates) is resolved by the compiler before execution; runtime polymorphism (virtual functions + inheritance) is resolved during program execution via vtable dispatch
Runtime polymorphism is always faster than compile-time polymorphism
Templates are a form of runtime polymorphism in C++
questions.answer: Compile-time polymorphism (function/operator overloading, templates) is resolved by the compiler before execution; runtime polymorphism (virtual functions + inheritance) is resolved during program execution via vtable dispatch

questions.question: What is dynamic memory allocation in C++ and when should it be preferred over stack allocation?
options: Dynamic allocation is always faster and should be used everywhere

Dynamic allocation (new/delete) allocates on the heap at runtime — preferred when object lifetime must outlive the creating function, when the size is unknown at compile time, or when large objects would overflow the stack
Dynamic allocation is only for primitive types; objects must always use stack allocation
Dynamic allocation should be avoided because the heap is not accessible in C++
questions.answer: Dynamic allocation (new/delete) allocates on the heap at runtime — preferred when object lifetime must outlive the creating function, when the size is unknown at compile time, or when large objects would overflow the stack

questions.question: What is function prototyping and what happens if a function is called before its definition without a prototype?

The compiler automatically finds the function definition anywhere in the file without a prototype
Function prototyping is optional in C++ and has no effect on compilation
Without a prototype, the function always returns 0
questions.answer: Without a prototype, the compiler assumes int return type and any argument types in older C; in C++ it is a compilation error — the function must be declared before use

questions.question: What is the role of the 'virtual' keyword in base class member functions?
options: virtual makes a function inline automatically

virtual enables runtime polymorphism — when a derived class overrides a virtual function, calling it through a base class pointer/reference invokes the derived version via vtable dispatch instead of the base version
virtual makes a function accessible from outside the class
virtual prevents a function from being called on an object directly — only through pointers
questions.answer: virtual enables runtime polymorphism — when a derived class overrides a virtual function, calling it through a base class pointer/reference invokes the derived version via vtable dispatch instead of the base version
